This leads to a compiler warning (e.g. https://launchpadlibrarian.net/839554212/buildlog_ubuntu-noble-amd64.wireshark_4.7.0-0~202512240643~ubuntu24.04.1_BUILDING.txt.gz)

```
In file included from <stdin>:275:
debian/libwsutil-dev/usr/include/wireshark/wsutil/socket.h:87:41: warning: ‘struct sockaddr_storage’ declared inside parameter list will not be visible outside of this definition or declaration
   87 | WS_DLL_PUBLIC int ws_socket_ptoa(struct sockaddr_storage *dst, const char *src, uint16_t def_port);
      |                                         ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

Which I believe is because when doing this check if all the public headers can be compiled that `HAVE_SYS_SOCKET_H` is not defined the way it is during a normal build, so `sys/socket.h` is not included, so this warning is produced as it looks like a new struct is being defined (which would cause a problem if another function did the same, because they would refer to possibly two different types.)

It's harmless here, but not defining various preprocessing defines that affect includes could cause actual problems in this check.

IMO the header is wrong. It should either include `sys/socket.h` (or equivalent) or forward declare `struct sockaddr_storage`. Public headers definitely should not have `HAVE_something_H` macros.

I realized that many public headers are still broken in some ways. The check is there to not deteriorate below the level again that's guarded by the check. Ideally the bar can be raised going forward, for example by adding a check for https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/issues/20901 , too.

Agreed. Apparently at one point it did include `config.h`, which was just wrong and correctly removed (d0a91b27f26762e9c998cc5e6fe71767de5d32c7) but not some checks that depended on it. (Presumably other code that included `wsutil/socket.h` was also including other headers.)

It's not true that public headers should not have header HAVE_ conditionals. That is generally the correct way to handle platform differences, rather than testing the platform and hard-coding assumptions.  Headers in isolation are not required to have all preprocessor symbols defined, nor be compilable with a misconfigured/empty build.

The actual problem is the Debian header check making incorrect assumptions.

Except that the conditionals are no longer (necessarily) defined when including that header after `config.h` was removed from it, which results in the struct not necessarily be defined, etc.

Or, as mentioned, the one struct could be forward declared as it's only used as a pointer, but part of the reason for this header in the first place is for code to be able to include it to get all the socket stuff without having to figure out what other headers to include.

> Except that the conditionals are no longer (necessarily) defined when including that header after `config.h` was removed from it, which results in the struct not necessarily be defined, etc.

`config.h` is included in the C file that also includes the public header. HAVE_ conditionals are always defined when the header is used in a correctly configured build, outside of artificial incomplete tests.

foo.c:
```
#include "config.h"
#include <wsutil/socket.h> // No compiler errors for this header with a correct build configuration
```

> Or, as mentioned, the one struct could be forward declared as it's only used as a pointer, but part of the reason for this header in the first place is for code to be able to include it to get all the socket stuff without having to figure out what other headers to include.

It is nice to abstract this in a single point of failure. Doesn't change the fact that at least once you need to figure out which headers need to be included.

If it's a public header theoretically used by plugins, do the plugins have to remember to include `config.h`? And if `config.h` always has to be included first to use the header, then why not restore it to the header as it was eight years ago?

The configuration header is specific to each build host and even translation unit. It's definitely not a public header. Yes out-of-tree plugins need to handle some configuration. It would be better not to have to do header checks for standard headers, that's just a practical constraint of trying to write portable software. If you only care about building for a single Linux distribution for some reason that's great, then obviously portability isn't a concern for you (general you) and the whole header check business is unnecessary complexity.

!22929 trades the requirement for build configuration for assumptions that are likely to fail for unusual platforms like Windows+MSYS. Not a good direction IMO.

> The configuration header is specific to each build host and even translation unit. It's definitely not a public header.

Anybody who ships libraries that have header files that require config.h has made a colossal mistake. (The gzip file I/O parts of libz did that, which caused some spectacularly hard-to-figure-out and annoying-to-fix issues in wiretap on OpenBSD. We no longer use those parts for reading capture files, which not only sped up random access to compressed files, it avoided dealing with that crock.)

Assume that your headers and libraries will be used by code that:

1. is being compiled by a different compiler (that, obviously, generates code that's "binary compatible" with the compiler that compiled your libraries, so you don't have to work around calling sequence/structure padding/etc. issues)
2. has its own config.h that might not define all the things your config.h defines and, if it *does* define them, might define them differently.
Even just for POSIX systems I have doubts that !22929 works well. BSD sockets and networking headers is just one area that is poorly standardized.

> Public headers definitely should not have `HAVE_something_H` macros.

...unless they define it themselves based on other #defines. Public headers must get all the information they need about the environment in which builds are being done directly from that environment, e.g. from 1) predefined macros, 2) `__has_attribute()`, and 3) other things that provide characteristics of that environment at build time rather than configure time.

> Even just for POSIX systems I have doubts that !22929 works well. BSD sockets and networking headers is just one area that is poorly standardized.

OK, let's look at the `HAVE_` macros being tested in wsutil/socket.h:

- `HAVE_UNISTD_H` - [if you're a POSIX system you have <unistd.h>](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/basedefs/unistd.h.html). That check is necessary only if we care about systems that 1) aren't POSIX systems and 2) don't define `_WIN32` or do define `__CYGWIN__`.
- `HAVE_ARPA_INET_H` - [if you're a POSIX system you have <arpa/inet.h>](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/basedefs/arpa/inet.h.html). Otherwise, if you're Windows you have <winsock2.h>. Are there any others?
- `HAVE_SYS_SOCKET_H` - [if you're a POSIX system you have <sys/socket.h>](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/basedefs/sys/socket.h.html). Otherwise, if you're Windows you have <winsock2.h>. Are there any others?
- `HAVE_NETINET_IN_H` - [if you're a POSIX system you have <netinet/in.h>](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/basedefs/netinet/in.h.html). Otherwise, if you're Windows you have <winsock2.h>. Are there any others?

And if you're not a passed-the-Single-UNIX-Specification-tests POSIX/UNIX system, but you're a UN\*X anyway, you're probably making an effort to be as close to POSIX as you can, so that doesn't leave the \*BSDs, or Linux distributions that *haven't* been run through the aforementioned tests, out in the cold. Heck, even [Haiku](https://www.haiku-os.org) probably looks POSIXy enough (and, yes, there *is* [a Wireshark port to Haiku](https://depot.haiku-os.org/__multipage/pkg/wireshark_gui/haikuports/haikuports_x86_64/4/2/6/-/1/x86_64?locale=en)).
C23 should, in theory, fix a lot of the nonsense by adding `__has_include`, which C++ already added earlier, which would be fine unlike expecting someone to include config.h in a plugin.

If your goal is to avoid plugins having to worry about portability, that is legitimate goal. Then I think you need to move all the portability checks into `wsutil/socket.c` and replace `struct sockaddr_storage` with a replacement type. This is what was done for `getopt()`.
Although, is this header really used by plugins? Probably not.

To conclude I think everyone recognizes that portability checks are not ideal, but that is not the same as being wrong and none of the solutions offered are better replacements. Something like Gnulib would be a proper fix (with its own issues maybe). `#ifdef WINDOWS #else` is not IMO.

Possibly plugins don't use it, and it shouldn't be a public header. It's mostly used by sharkd. But it is and config.h was removed from it in your mass "remove config.h from public headers" commit, leaving it in a broken state.

There are one or two dissectors that use socket includes for some reason. Having a common header might be easier for those than each dissector having to figure out exactly how to make sockets work, and if a dissector can use it, so might a plugin.

My commit absolutely did not leave it in a broken state. That was intentional, as I tried to explain. The fact that nothing was broken other than an IMO flawed test is evidence enough.

I'm not arguing against having the sockets header. It was working fine, and now after 65d36007b231139ffad43284a569caed86bc7c71 it is still working for the platforms we test on but less fine.

> Then I think you need to move all the portability checks into `wsutil/socket.c`

Exactly.

> `#ifdef WINDOWS #else` is not IMO.

Given that [Microsoft's compilers don't define `WINDOWS` if the target is "modern" (as in "not 16-bit") Windows](https://github.com/cpredef/predef/blob/master/OperatingSystems.md#windows), no, `#ifdef WINDOWS` ... `#else` ... `#endif` won't work.

`#ifdef _WIN32`, however, will work in a header.

Providing APIs that work on multiple platforms is, so that the code *using* your library doesn't have to have its *own* platform tests at compile time, is best. However, that might be done, in part or in whole, by compile-time platform tests in header files, so I have no problem with using `#ifdef _WIN32` in header files. See, for example, wsutil/file_util.h - no need to add an extra layer of procedure call just to avoid using platform tests in the header file.

> The fact that nothing was broken other than an IMO flawed test is evidence enough.

It was not broken on an build of the repository of various in-tree programs and dissectors like shark_session that include `config.h` themselves first.

It would, I think, be broken if someone tried to do an out-of-tree build of a separate plugin or anything else using that header, and expected to be able to just include that header without generating their own `config.h` and adding all the various `HAVE_` defines. It's true that no one complained about that exactly, and I agree that I don't know if it needs to be a public header, but I don't think it's reasonable to expect people to include a sufficiently similar `config.h` in an out-of-tree compilation of some external plugin.

> There are one or two dissectors that use socket includes for some reason.

Which dissectors are doing that? They may be doing it for a reason, but the first question is "is it a *good* reason?" For example, using it to get `AF_` values to use when *dissecting*, rather than when binding or connecting a socket, is *not* a good reason, as `AF_` values depend on the platform for which you're compiling. epan/dissectors/packet-null.c doesn't use the platform's `AF_` values, it uses `BSD_AF_` values that *we* design, based on the values that various BSDs (including CupertinoBSD) have. See epan/aftypes.h.

> It would, I think, be broken if someone tried to do an out-of-tree build of a separate plugin or anything else using that header, and expected to be able to just include that header without generating their own `config.h` and adding all the various `HAVE_` defines.

And if they do that, but don't happen, for whatever reason, to define those `HAVE_` defines *in the same way that our build process does*, and things fail for mysterious reasons, that means that obliging the build process of third-party plugins to 1) use a configuration process that generates a config.h file and 2) have that process generate particular `HAVE_` defines - _**AND document which defines those are**_ - may not be sufficient.

> It's true that no one complained about that exactly, and I agree that I don't know if it needs to be a public header, but I don't think it's reasonable to expect people to include a sufficiently similar `config.h` in an out-of-tree compilation of some external plugin.

I think it is reasonable if they want to use a socket header that requires it for reasons. Expectations are just that. They can be wrong. A header with a HAVE_ conditional makes that part of the public interface. This is not ideal and should be avoided and can't change the surface of the API but otherwise it is allowed if it solves a real-world portability issue. Otherwise the correct action is obviously to just remove the condition (not replace it with a more fragile test).

By the way using a pre-processor conditional that your compiler defines for you (e.g: _WIN32) or one that your build system defines in a configuration header or one you are expected to define manually is not that different. They are all just compile time configuration. Using a macro symbol for headers is less convenient because usually the compiler won't handle it for you but more reliable and flexible. The convenience factor doesn't magically make one OK and the other wrong.

> And if they do that, but don't happen, for whatever reason, to define those `HAVE_` defines _in the same way that our build process does_, and things fail for mysterious reasons, that means that obliging the build process of third-party plugins to 1) use a configuration process that generates a config.h file and 2) have that process generate particular `HAVE_` defines - **_AND document which defines those are_** - may not be sufficient.

It is sufficient, unless a colossal mistake was made.

> Which dissectors are doing that? 

https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-lbm.h

I'm not sure that it really needs to. It looks like the only reason is in order to get `IN_MULTICAST`, and `wsutil/inet_addr.h` has in4_addr_is_multicast that is probably fit for that purpose.

> I think it is reasonable if they want to use a socket header that requires it for reasons.

If the reasons why it requires a config.h are themselves reasonable.

> Expectations are just that. They can be wrong.

And I consider an expectation that people using your library will be fine with having to provide a config.h file telling the header what the target platform's characteristics are is, at minimum, unwise and impolite, and possibly even wrong.

> By the way using a pre-processor conditional that your compiler defines for you (e.g: \_WIN32) or one that your build system defines in a configuration header or one you are expected to define manually is not that different.

Developers don't have to do any work to get the compiler to define `_WIN32`. They *do* have to do work to ensure that a `HAVE_` is properly defined. I consider that a significant difference.

> Using a macro symbol for headers is less convenient because usually the compiler won't handle it for you but more reliable and flexible.

It's only as reliable as the entity that defines, or doesn't define, it. If it's a header local to a project, then the project's configuration tools and files are the entity in question, so it's as reliable as the configuration tools and files *maintained by the project* are. If it's a *public* header, then, when some *other* project is using that header, it's only as reliable as *that project's developers*, and you have only limited control, at best, over that (i.e., you can tell them what they need to do, and if you do a good job of that, that's a start, but you can't control whether they correctly understand what you tell them).

> The convenience factor doesn't magically make one OK and the other wrong.

The convenience factor may replace "some random other project's developers" with "the developers of the platform's development tools"; I trust the latter more than I trust the former.

> > And if they do that, but don't happen, for whatever reason, to define those `HAVE_` defines _in the same way that our build process does_, and things fail for mysterious reasons, that means that obliging the build process of third-party plugins to 1) use a configuration process that generates a config.h file and 2) have that process generate particular `HAVE_` defines - **_AND document which defines those are_** - may not be sufficient.
> 
> It is sufficient, unless a colossal mistake was made.

Here's an example of the consequences of exactly such a colossal mistake; this is why I'm as adamant as I am about using `HAVE_` defines in public header files:

https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/6fa0fd5fa8fccae84fec5db4094f3a2dc7a82d2b/wiretap/file_wrappers.c#L28

That colossal mistake by the zlib developers is what I was referring to in https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/22752#note_2973910134.

If I ever encounter a mistake that colossal mistake in the future, I will track somebody down, explain it to them, and inform them that if it ever happens again, somebody's head will be removed and placed on a pike.

> Here's an example of the consequences of exactly such a colossal mistake; this is why I'm as adamant as I am about using `HAVE_` defines in public header files:

You do not have to tell me, I already fixed it in Wireshark's code base (d0a91b27f26762e9c998cc5e6fe71767de5d32c7).

The mistake is including `zconf.h` in a public header. not using `#ifdef HAVE_whatever`.

> The mistake is including `zconf.h` in a public header.

In zlib 1.1.3, the version of zlib at the time of that cluster@#!@, zconf.h *is* a public header of the library. (Srsly, look at the Makefile - it installs it, along with zutil.h. zconf.h isn't zlib's equivalent of config.h, Makefile is zlib's equivalent of config.h - the configure script sets the `-D` flags in the Makefile. zconf.h is, instead, the header file that, using a lot of platform predefines, as well as some `HAVE_` values, defines a bunch of configuration values.)

> not using `#ifdef HAVE_whatever`.

This isn't a binary choice. There are at least three options.

1. You can choose not to require that a project specify `HAVE_` variables to inform your library's headers of the platform configuration. This imposes the least requirements upon users of your library, thus providing them with fewer opportunities to get it wrong. Given that, when they get it wrong, there's a good chance that they will report it to *the library developers* as a problem, I prefer that solution, if it's possible to implement.
2. If it's impossible to implement the first solution, you can require them to specify those variables, document what they have to do as clearly as possible should do as good a job as possible of telling them how to do this, and, if you can, you should provide ways to catch errors if they do it incorrectly, as that may help them get it right *before* they a problem to the library's developers.
3. Or you can cluster@#!@ the whole thing the way the zlib developers and the \*BSD developers did.

In the case of zlib, they needed to define `z_off_t` as the file offset data type for the gzio routines. They wanted it to match `off_t` on platforms that have `off_t`; they chose to use "platforms that have unistd.h" as being "platforms that have `off_t`.

On all other platforms, they defined `z_off_t` as `long`.

You can't use "`_POSIX_VERSION` is defined" as a way of saying "this is a POSIX system and thus has unistd.h", because `_POSIX_VERSION` is defined by... unistd.h.

Enumerating UN\*Xes with various predefines would probably have required a lot of predefines to test at the time (before some of those UN\*Xes disappeared), and some of them may not have had predefines.

Enumerating *non*-UN\*Xes might have worked. [Back at that time, they had a number of non-UN\*Xes that they supported](https://web.archive.org/web/20010707004717/http://www.gzip.org/zlib/); *if* they all had predefines, they could have used that. zconf.h definitely *does* check for some OSes with predefines.

But even what they did would have worked *if they had bothered to explicitly state that, if you're going to use zlib on a platform that has unistd.h, *you must define `HAVE_UNISTD_H` before including any zlib headers*. [Their documentation at the time](https://web.archive.org/web/20010627154319/http://www.gzip.org/zlib/manual.html) did *not* do so.

I.e., not only did they avoid doing possibility 1) above, they also avoided doing possibility 2), and thus ended up doing possibility 3) and cluster@#!@ed.

This was made worse by it being platform-dependent whether `HAVE_UNISTD_H` was defined when zlib was built, and thus making it platform-dependent whether `z_off_t` is defined as `off_t` or as `long`, so, for a user of zlib, appropriately defining `HAVE_UNISTD_H` means "figuring out what it was on the platform for which you're building your zlib-using software *at the time zlib was built*", which may *not* match whether your platform has unistd.h, so it's *not* as easy as using your project's config.h file.

(And, no, making zlib's config.h file a public header wouldn't do the trick. zlib doesn't *have* a config.h file; the configure script modifies the `-D` flags in the Makefile.)

Also, for whatever reason, this doesn't seem to produced the same errors either at the CI here or at the GitHub CI as at Ubuntu launchpad. There is an error message at GitHub: 

```
Built target install-headers
E: dh_python3 dh_python3:176: no package to act on (python3-foo or one with ${python3:Depends} in Depends)
```

but I don't know if that's during this step or immediately afterwards.

That's fixed in Debian's packaging. `python3:any` should be `${python3:Depends}` in `packaging/debian/control`. I did not want to duplicate all the small fixes in packaging, thus tried to start a conversation about syncing it from Debian at https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/issues/20351#note_2791572025 .
